summary: Creates a registry for describing the types of places a human or end system might be found. Other protocols can use these common terms as constants, with examples like aircraft, office and train station. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shared word list for kinds of places, such as office or train station, so different programs use the same words.

questions: what is the location types registry
what are the location type tokens
how do i register a new location type
subtitle: A shared list of tokens such as office, classroom and train-station for describing the kind of place a device is in.

tldr.problem: Protocols that tell a device where it is need a common vocabulary for kinds of places, beyond a street address or coordinates, so the device can adapt its behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of location type tokens from 'aircraft' to 'watercraft', publishes them as an IANA registry and an XML schema, and adds new tokens through Expert Review.
tldr.outcome: Other protocols can reference these tokens as constants. The RFC itself does not say how they are used; other documents do that.

today: RFC 4589 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The text points to other documents for how the tokens are used.

sections.title: Why a Registry of Place Types
sections.content:
RFC 4589 creates a registry of location type tokens. The expectation is that the network, through configuration or management protocols, tells a mobile device what kind of place it is in, and the device tailors its behavior. For example, terms such as classroom, place-of-worship and theater could let a phone switch from ringer to vibrate. A street address or coordinates alone would generally not allow that decision.

The terms are meant to be in common use across cultures and countries, roughly matching the level of detail on maps. The registration process lets the list grow while trying to prevent an unnecessary explosion in the registry.

The RFC does not say how the values are used. Other documents do: one describes carrying them in DHCP, another conveys them from a RADIUS client to a RADIUS server, and rich presence (RPID) also uses them.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone knows where it is on a map, but not whether that spot is a library or a theater. This list gives names to those kinds of places.

sections.title: Tokens, Overlap and Combinations
sections.content:
Using tokens (protocol constants) makes it easier to build systems across multiple languages, since a user interface can translate a finite set of tokens into text or icons. Protocols using the registry are encouraged to add free-text fields, with language and character set labels, for location types that are not registered.

The registry does not try to be a hierarchy, except in special cases. restaurant is defined to include cafe, and public encompasses street, public-transport, aircraft, bus, bus-station, train, train-station, airport, shopping-area, outdoors and watercraft. Generic terms help when detail is unavailable or privacy suggests a less precise term.

A place may have several terms at once, such as restaurant and airport. The registry puts no limit on combinations and leaves the number of terms per protocol element to the using protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A place can wear more than one label, like a cafe inside an airport. Some labels are bigger boxes that hold smaller ones, such as "public".

sections.title: The Location Types
sections.content:
The tokens describe where an entity is. The entity can be a person or an object such as a network access point or end system. Each token has a short definition. They fall into a few rough groups:

  • Vehicles: aircraft, automobile, bicycle, bus, motorcycle, train, truck, watercraft.
  • Transport places: airport, bus-station, train-station, parking.
  • Work, civic and learning: office, government, bank, school, classroom, library, hospital, prison, industrial, construction, warehouse.
  • Leisure and commerce: arena, stadium, theater, club, bar, cafe, restaurant, hotel, store, shopping-area, convention-center, place-of-worship.
  • Open and general: outdoors, street, water, public, public-transport, residence, underway.
  • Catch-alls: other (a place without a registered type) and unknown (the type is not known).

Some definitions are deliberately broad. For example, residence is a private setting, not necessarily the entity's own home, and theater covers auditoriums and classrooms too. Some definitions derive from the Merriam-Webster Online Dictionary.
sections.plainLanguage: The list has names for cars and planes, schools and shops, parks and streets, plus "other" and "unknown" for when nothing fits.

sections.title: Tokens and the XML Schema
sections.content:
The registry can be used in two ways: as a list of tokens referenced by protocols that accept textual tokens, and as an XML schema with its own namespace, referenced by other schemas explicitly or via namespace="##other".

The schema's target namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:location-type. It declares one element per token. Every element has an empty type except other, which has a string type with an xml:lang attribute so a short note can be attached. The schema as printed spells the bicycle element bicyle, while the token list in the RFC uses bicycle.
sections.plainLanguage: The same list also comes as a computer-readable form. Each place name is a little box, and only "other" lets you write a note inside.

sections.title: How IANA Maintains the Registry
sections.content:
The document creates new IANA registries for the location types in Section 3, starting with aircraft and finishing with watercraft. IANA keeps the registry both as an XML schema and as a list of tokens, with the same content.

New tokens are assigned after Expert Review, following RFC 2434. The expert generally consults the GEOPRIV working group mailing list or its successor. Updates and deletions follow the same procedure. Tokens should not be specific to a country, region, organization or company, and should be well defined and widely recognized. Tokens MUST follow the XML Names character set restrictions.

Each registration includes a Token Identifier, a Description (with examples where the term covers several more precise terms) and an XML namespace, typically urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:location-type:ext where ext is the extension name. The tokens are not limited to XML: the Token Identifier is the XML element content, not the element name. The document also registers the namespace URN and the schema, with the IESG as registrant for the schema.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new place name, an expert checks that it is useful everywhere and not just for one company or country. Then it goes on the official list.

sections.title: Internationalization and Security
sections.content:
The location type values MUST NOT be presented to the user. They behave like tokens or tags, so no internationalization support is required; a user interface is expected to map them to suitable text or icons.

The security section is a single sentence: because the document only defines a registry of location types, it does not raise security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The words are meant for programs, not for showing on screen. Programs turn them into words or pictures in the right language. The list itself is not a security risk.

items.text: Typically urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:location-type:ext, where ext is the extension name.
